body.text: The signing of the Australia–Solomon Islands Treaty on 25 November capped a remarkable six-month period in which Honiara’s strategic orientation shifted markedly, bilateral relations were reset, and the two countries agreed on a new level of ambition.

The key to Australia’s success was being prepared for inevitable Pacific shifts, the big one being Matthew Wale becoming Solomons prime minister in May. Wale moved quickly to rebuild ties after his election, reflecting enduring trust and goodwill towards Australia in Honiara and unease over the China-favouring approach of former prime ministers Manasseh Sogavare and Jeremiah Manele.

Canberra’s ability to capitalise on this so quickly underlines the commitment of Australian ministers and officials to our Pacific neighbours’ needs and the challenge of permanent contest with China in the region.

And it goes to the heart of the government’s two-speed China policy, composed of public–facing diplomatic euphoria and a behind-the-scenes security and deterrence posture geared for ‘disagreeing where we must’.

The treaty follows a startling run of success for Canberra in negotiating agreements with Tuvalu, Nauru and Vanuatu and alliances with Papua New Guinea and Fiji. Collectively, these efforts reflect Canberra’s recognition that Australia’s challenges are connected with those of its neighbours and require integrated responses.

For Honiara, the partnership brings economic, development and institutional support, as well as a trusted security partner. And it reflects an attempt to draw a line in the sand domestically on Honiara’s foreign policy: Wale described the treaty as a major step towards ending the uncertainty that had characterised his country’s regional relationships. For Canberra, a stable, capable and friendly Solomon Islands is vital to Australia’s security and to its broader interests in a peaceful, prosperous and resilient Pacific.

Australia’s experience with the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands, which ran from 2003 to 2017 and cost about A$3 billion, underscores the consequences of instability. The deaths of Australian Protective Service Officer Adam Dunning and Private Jamie Clark during the mission have been reminders that securing peace involves sacrifices greater than the financial costs of maintaining it.

A deteriorating international security environment – correctly diagnosed by Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong in her speech to Parliament on Tuesday – has also elevated the importance of trust and reassurance. Australia’s longstanding ties and institutional and community relationships in the Pacific are a foundation that China cannot easily replicate.

Australia’s integration agenda recognises that long-term stability depends on economic opportunity, strong institutions and human development. Integration also provides a necessary inoculation against the converging threats and malign interests that now characterise the more dangerous world we live in.

The treaty signed on 25 November provides A$740 million to Solomon Islands over 10 years, according to a government source. Much of that is focused on building human capital, including support for Wale’s free education policy. Other initiatives cover health, infrastructure, energy, connectivity, climate resilience, governance and employment, with expanded opportunities under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme for temporary work in Australia.

Provisions on transparency, accountability, corruption prevention and nationally determined priorities aim to make assistance sustainable and strengthen institutions. They also set a standard that narrower foreign interests will find difficult to live up to. For example, the opaque and controversial Constituency Development Funds will now be tied to public management initiatives supported by the World Bank.

As for the strategic dimension, Solomon Islands lies about 2,000 km northeast of Australia. Its geography, long strategically consequential to Canberra, could be crucial in a crisis in which Australia would need to protect regional sea lanes, support allied operations and prevent an adversary from establishing an unfettered military presence in the Pacific.

The treaty satisfactorily addresses these concerns, reinforcing Australia’s role as Solomon Islands’ primary security partner and committing to strengthening intelligence cooperation and the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force (there is no military), while providing for consultation on sensitive infrastructure and security cooperation with countries outside the Pacific Islands Forum.

Of greatest significance, it affirms Solomon Islands’ sovereign decision that there will be no foreign military or security bases on its territory and contains a provision – Article 5, clause 5c – to ‘ensure security cooperation comes from Pacific Islands Forum members’. This otherwise innocuous reference likely sits behind the reported decision by Wale’s government not to renew the 2022 Solomon Islands–China security agreement when it expires in April 2027. Australia is a member of the forum. China isn’t.

The treaty is a great outcome for both nations, the sort of ‘win-win cooperation’ that some countries can only talk about. It will make the difference between a stable, well-governed and more prosperous region – meeting our decades-long national interests – and a region in which external powers shape outcomes for their global agendas at the expense of those of us who live here.

But the permanent contest with China for influence guarantees impermanence. Beijing will respond. It retains economic interests, political relationships – likely mobilised in the motion of no confidence filed against Wale in August – and the capacity to cultivate influence. There will inevitably be efforts to challenge the new direction, particularly given the domestic political pressures facing Wale’s government.

So Australia cannot afford to rest on its diplomatic achievement. It must now show that its partnership improves Solomon Islanders’ lives, respects their sovereignty and responds to their priorities. The treaty provides a framework for doing precisely that.
